results.title: Why AI Alignment Requires Peircean Semiosis
results.content: # Language Models’ Hall of Mirrors Problem: Why AI Alignment Requires Peircean Semiosis. + Published by Springer Nature in Philosophy & Technology. This paper examines some limitations of large language models (LLMs) through the framework of Peircean semiotics. We argue that basic LLMs exist within a “hall of mirrors,” reflecting only the linguistic surface of training data without indexical grounding in a shared external world, and manipulating symbols without participation in socially-mediated epistemology. We then argue that newer developments, including extended context windows, persistent memory, and mediated interactions with reality, are moving towards making newer Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems into genuine Peircean interpretants, and conclude that LLMs may be approaching this goal, and we identify no fundamental architectural barriers that would prevent this. This lens reframes a central challenge for AI alignment: without grounding in the semiotic process, a model’s linguistic encoding of goals may diverge from real-world values. * The bewitching AI: The Illusion of Communication with Large Language Models.

results.title: How Language Models Reflect Our Semiotic Theories
results.content: As AI researcher Melanie Mitchell (2019) explains in her book *Artificial Intelligence: A Guide for Thinking Humans,* these systems learn “a vast web of associations, a kind of statistical map of how language is used, rather than learning what words actually mean in terms of experiences in the world” (p. Perhaps language models, in analyzing the patterns of human language, are accessing precisely this environmental scaffold that connects our embodied experience to our abstract thought — not replicating embodied understanding but exploiting its traces in linguistic structure. Rather than seeing language models as purely Saussurean entities entirely divorced from the grounded understanding that Peirce described, we might view them as specialized processors of the differential aspects of meaning that nonetheless indirectly access aspects of embodied cognition through their analysis of human language. Language models, in their remarkable simulation of human-like understanding without direct experience, reveal both the power of differential semantics and its limitations.
